And the predator felt the cage closing in. Chapter 5: Fault Lines The campfire burned steady, sparks drifting upward into the endless dark, fading against the faint silhouettes of the treetops. Survivors lingered in wary silence, jittery in the aftermath of something they didn’t fully understand. The tension of the last match hadn’t fully left their muscles; the regular flow of the trial having been so dramatically altered from what they had come to expect that nobody was quite sure how to fully let it go. Dwight sat near the edge of the circle, spine too straight, hands tight on his knees. He wasn’t trembling, exactly, but his body hadn’t decided if it was entirely safe to uncoil yet. His breath came short, shallow. His glasses reflected the flames in little red glints that flickered and danced. He hadn’t said a word since they got back. Not until Jake broke the silence. “Are you gonna tell us what happened,” he asked, more edge than joke, “or just sit there like you saw the devil? You look like he damn near ripped you in half back there.” His tone was half-amused, but the tension betrayed him. Sure, Dwight had more anxiety than most of them, but none of them had seen him look quite like that before — pale, wide-eyed, barely able to stand after the trial ended. Dwight swallowed. His voice was quiet. “He had me.” “Wesker?” Feng asked, eyebrow raised. “So what? He always has you.” “No,” Dwight said quickly. “No, not like that. He had me— lifted. One hand. Slammed me into the wall, and then...” He hesitated, frowning against the memory, trying to find the words. His fingers flexed once, then clenched again. “Something stopped him. I don’t know how else to explain it. It was just us, and he completely had me, and then he just... let go. Not on purpose. It was like something hit him. Hard.” A silence fell over the fire. Jake exhaled slowly, arms crossed. “That... doesn’t sound like him.” “He’s been off,” Claudette murmured, almost to herself. “The last few matches. I thought it was just an off day or something, but... his swings are weird. Delayed. Off-balance.” “I thought I was imagining it,” Feng added. “But when I looped him by the greenhouse, he full- on missed a corner he never misses. Like, by a mile.” Jake grinned faintly. “Sounds like a win to me.” But his smile didn’t reach his eyes. None of theirs did. Something in them knew it wasn’t just sloppiness. Not really. Dwight’s knuckles whitened. “There’s something on his wrist. I saw it when he grabbed me. A band. Black, with these little red lights. It was glowing — sparking — when he dropped me. And his face...” He stopped again. Claudette turned toward him, tone soft. “What about it?” Dwight shook his head slowly, like the image still lingered somewhere behind his eyes. “It didn’t look like him. It looked —” He didn’t finish. He didn’t have to. The word hung in the air anyway, unspoken but understood. Human. The fire cracked, a log splitting with a sharp pop. “Well,” Meg said finally, arms folded tight across her chest, “regardless of what’s going on... it’s not our problem.” That earned her a few sideways glances, but she barreled forward. “I’m just saying. If something’s wrong with him — whatever that means — then that’s good news for us. We might actually survive a match without getting punched through a generator. I’m not gonna cry over it.” “It’s not about that,” Claudette said, her voice uneasy, “I don’t think it’s that simple.” “It kind of is,” Jake muttered. Dwight looked thoughtful for a moment. His fingers drummed once on his knee and stopped. His eyes stayed locked on the fire. “It felt like...” he started, then trailed off. He couldn’t explain the feeling in his chest when Wesker dropped him. Not fear. Not relief. Something worse. The afterimage of being gripped by something so powerful it could’ve crushed him without thought — and then realizing it tried and still couldn’t. That moment of recoil. The mask slipping. The confusion. The pain. And still, the man had looked him in the eye like a feral thing in a trap. Like it wasn’t just about failing to kill — it was about losing the choice. Dwight shivered. Claudette glanced sideways, picking nervously at the hem of her sleeve. “Do you think someone’s doing it on purpose?” “To him?” Jake frowned. “Why not?” she asked. “They mess with us all the time. Maybe someone is trying to balance the playing field.” “Sounds like they’re doing us a solid,” Meg muttered. Silence crept in again, stretching thin and uneasy. Across the Fog, beneath flickering fluorescents and old concrete, Wesker sat alone in the RPD’s western hallway. One elbow braced on his knee, wrist resting loosely in his other hand. The cuff hummed. Not loudly — not anymore. It didn’t have to. It pulsed like a second heart now, a low throb beneath skin and bone, threading into every twitch of seared, aching muscle. He knew they were talking about him. Didn’t need to hear the words. The Fog carried more than blood and footsteps. It carried intent. And something in the firelight across the way was pricking at him like needles behind the eyes. They thought he was slipping. They thought he was weak. And somewhere, just beneath the wires — behind the intercom crackle and rustling vents — came the faintest wheeze of laughter, as if Herman could hear it too. Chapter 6 - Judgement The next trial began with the usual surge of anticipation — Wesker stepped forward into the harsh sunlight of Coldwind, Uroboros stirring beneath his skin like a tide ready to break. He welcomed the power, clung to it. It was the last thread
